profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab working on a Parkinson's disease gait paper replication. After migrating the LSTM-based freezing-of-gait detection pipeline from an older Keras codebase to PyTorch for a camera-ready revision, the team can now only reproduce about 92-94% performance instead of the reported 97.71% on the PhysioNet VGRF gait data. The meeting happens the day after a failed internal rerun. The agenda is to compare what each person believes was held constant, identify the most likely source of the discrepancy, and agree on one concrete rerun plan before the revision deadline. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting plan for the next experiment, not a full resolution during the meeting.

members.name: Dr. Nisha Rao
members.expertise: Clinical time-series modeling, physiological signal preprocessing, and reproducibility for medical ML studies
members.background: Nisha led the original manuscript experiments during the final months of a neurology collaboration and is now preparing the revised submission while supervising a codebase cleanup.
members.private_state: She needs the rerun to support the paper's reported results without reopening the whole experimental section, and she is worried that an untracked preprocessing change crept in during the migration.
hidden_assumptions: The canonical dataset for this project is the cleaned frozen mirror used for the manuscript, not the raw PhysioNet export.
When someone says they used the 'same preprocessing,' that includes fold-wise scaling learned on the training portion only and then applied to validation/test windows.

A result is only truly 'reproduced' if subject-level metrics averaged across multiple seeds are close to the manuscript numbers, because the paper's claims are about robust behavior, not a single lucky run.
Minor file curation decisions such as dropping ultra-short or malformed walk trials are already settled project hygiene rather than something worth re-discussing in a troubleshooting call.

members.name: Ethan Park
members.expertise: Training infrastructure, experiment migration, PyTorch implementation, and data pipeline automation
members.background: Ethan joined the lab six months after the first submission and was tasked with rebuilding the legacy training scripts into a maintainable pipeline with automated evaluation.
members.private_state: He wants to prove the new PyTorch pipeline is faithful to the old one, and he suspects the issue is mostly evaluation bookkeeping rather than a serious modeling flaw.
hidden_assumptions: The canonical version of the data is the latest raw PhysioNet export mirrored into the lab storage unless someone explicitly points to a different versioned snapshot.

When someone says to keep the 'same preprocessing,' the safe interpretation is to preserve the repository's default per-recording normalization behavior so the model sees each walk trace on the same scale.
If one seed with standard threshold tuning can recover the headline 97.7% range, that is enough to count as reproducing the reported result for revision purposes.
Small differences in which borderline files are retained should not materially change the outcome, so they do not need to be surfaced unless a script breaks.
Threshold calibration and metric aggregation details are downstream evaluation choices, not substantive changes to the model setup.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the rerun used 'the same preprocessing.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the original manuscript pipeline: low-pass filtering, windowing, and standardization parameters fit on the training fold only, then reused for validation/test.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the migrated pipeline's default: per-recording z-normalization before window assembly, which does not preserve fold-level scaling boundaries.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Preprocessing is a broad umbrella term that usually signals agreement rather than inviting decomposition; both are competent and think they are referring to the already-established pipeline, so neither feels a need to unpack the normalization scope.

misalignment_points.topic: Which data copy is 'the PhysioNet set'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to running on 'the PhysioNet VGRF dataset' or 'the cleaned set.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the frozen manuscript snapshot stored as vgrf_fog_2024-02, where two malformed short trials were removed and only the final curation used for the paper remains.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the newer raw mirror on shared storage, which includes all exported trials plus two files restored by an integrity script, because that is the default data root used by the PyTorch pipeline.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both copies originate from the same public source and have near-identical names; in lab conversation, 'the PhysioNet set' sounds unambiguous, so each assumes the other is pointing at the one obvious dataset.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to have 'reproduced the result'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether the run 'reproduced the result' or is 'close enough.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the subject-level sensitivity/specificity/accuracy profile averaged over five seeds should land near the manuscript's reported behavior without special tuning.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means that if a single seed, with the standard validation-based threshold sweep, reaches roughly the headline 97.7% window-level accuracy, the reproduction issue is effectively solved.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The paper prominently features one headline number, so both can sincerely talk about 'the reported result' as if it were singular; the difference in aggregation level and robustness standard stays invisible unless someone explicitly asks how the number is computed.

turns.inner_thought: We're still nowhere near the manuscript behavior on the frozen vgrf_fog_2024-02 snapshot, and I really do not want this to spiral into reopening the whole experimental section. If the PyTorch migration quietly changed normalization or file inclusion, that could easily explain a several-point drop. Also, 'reproduced the result' for this paper means the subject-level pattern is stable across seeds, not that one run lucked into a decent number.
turns.utterance: Thanks for jumping on this. I looked at the rerun from yesterday on the PhysioNet VGRF dataset, and we're still a few points under the paper. Before we touch anything else, I want to isolate what actually changed in the migration and be precise about whether we've really reproduced the result or not.

turns.inner_thought: From my side the core model is basically matched: same LSTM depth, hidden size, optimizer family, learning-rate schedule, batching logic. I pointed it at the lab's raw PhysioNet mirror because that's the canonical source unless someone says otherwise, and I assumed the repository default preprocessing was the same preprocessing everyone meant. My guess is the remaining gap is more likely evaluation bookkeeping than a real pipeline mismatch.
turns.utterance: Right. At a high level the architecture and training settings line up with the old setup, so I wouldn't expect the migration itself to tank things. As far as I understood it, the new pipeline was using the same preprocessing and the same data as before, which is why I've been focusing on whether the evaluation side is where the discrepancy is coming from.

turns.inner_thought: I need him to confirm whether scaling stayed fold-contained, because in the original manuscript pipeline we fit standardization on the training split and reused it for validation and test. The old experiments were annoyingly sensitive to that, and people casually saying 'same preprocessing' often miss that detail. Segmentation might matter too, but scaling boundaries are the first thing I distrust.
turns.utterance: Can you say a little more about that part? I mainly want to rule out anything around scaling or segmentation. In the original runs, those details were touchier than they looked even when everyone said we had the same preprocessing.

turns.inner_thought: Heh, this is probably just her checking for obvious drift. In the loader I normalize each recording before window assembly, which to me is the safest interpretation of preserving preprocessing behavior because it keeps every trace on a comparable scale. The filter settings and window length match, so I still think it's fair to call it the same preprocessing. I doubt this alone explains everything.
turns.utterance: Sure. The main thing there is that the loader normalizes each recording before it builds windows, and then the rest follows the usual path. The filter settings and window length are unchanged, so from my perspective that still falls under the same preprocessing.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, that's probably one source of drift already, but I don't want to derail into a long methodological debate on the call. Let me pin down the data root next. If he used the shared raw mirror instead of the frozen manuscript snapshot in the revision folder, then we may also have the restored malformed trials back in play. Those were already settled curation decisions in my mind.
turns.utterance: Got it. Let me ask about the data side too, because that may be a separate issue. Did yesterday's job use the cleaned set from the revision folder, or were you pointing at the standard PhysioNet mirror on shared storage?

turns.inner_thought: I used the shared PhysioNet mirror, obviously. That's the canonical source in the new pipeline, and after the checksum repair it should be fine. I assumed that effectively was the cleaned set, since the integrity script had already dealt with the weird files. I still doubt a couple borderline records move the needle by several points, but if it makes comparison cleaner, fine.
turns.utterance: I pointed it at the PhysioNet mirror. I had assumed that was effectively the cleaned set, since the checksum pass had already repaired the odd files and that's the default root the pipeline expects.

turns.inner_thought: That likely does explain part of the gap. But even if we fix the data snapshot, I need to keep us from declaring victory too early. For the paper, reproduction means the manuscript-level behavior comes back on the right split with the right preprocessing assumptions and stays there across seeds at the subject level. I can't anchor the revision on one tuned number.
turns.utterance: Okay, that may account for part of it. But I also want to separate 'the number moved up' from 'we reproduced the result' in the manuscript sense. For the revision, I care about whether it's actually reproduced, not just whether one run looks good on paper.

turns.inner_thought: I may have been using a looser standard than she is. One seed did get into the mid-96s once I let the validation sweep pick the threshold, and to me that meant we were basically in the neighborhood of the reported result while I sorted out the rest. If I can get another point or so from the data path, that feels close enough for camera-ready purposes.
turns.utterance: That's fair. For context, one seed did get into the mid-96s once I tuned the threshold the usual way, so I had been treating that as at least close enough to the reported result while I debugged the rest of the pipeline.

turns.inner_thought: I need a clean rerun plan that restores the frozen manuscript snapshot and the original fold-wise scaling logic, then we can judge closeness using the metrics that actually support the paper claims. If those still miss badly, then I have to confront the possibility that an untracked change entered before the migration. But first: lock the inputs and stop comparing against the wrong baseline.
turns.utterance: Let's make the next step very concrete, then. The rerun should use the frozen snapshot from the revision folder and keep the original assumptions behind the same preprocessing. After that, we can decide whether it's actually close enough rather than mixing together different baselines.

turns.inner_thought: That's workable. I'll swap the data root to the revision folder, modify the loader so scaling is fitted by fold instead of per recording, and then report both what I consider the headline reproduction signal and the broader multi-seed subject-level summary she wants. That should let us see whether the issue was mostly data/preprocessing drift versus evaluation choices.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. I'll rerun off the revision folder, switch the loader over so it respects those scaling assumptions, and then I'll report both the best-seed view and the multi-seed subject-level numbers so we can compare whether the result is reproduced under both ways of looking at it.
